content: Serum sickness is a hypersensitivity reaction that occurs in response to an antiserum derived from an animal source. It is classified as a type III hypersensitivity reaction, which involves immune complex formation. The condition typically manifests within ten days following exposure to the antiserum, and its symptoms resemble those of an allergic reaction. However, unlike anaphylaxis, the onset of serum sickness symptoms is delayed, usually occurring 2 to 4 weeks after exposure. The pathophysiology of serum sickness involves the administration of animal-derived antibodies, often used to prevent infections. The human immune system may misidentify the proteins in the antiserum as harmful antigens, triggering the production of antibodies. These antibodies bind to the foreign proteins, forming immune complexes. These complexes can deposit in tissues and elicit further immune responses, leading to the symptoms associated with serum sickness. Additionally, certain medications, such as penicillin-based drugs and lincomycin hydrochloride, can also induce serum sickness. The symptoms of serum sickness may take up to 14 days to appear after exposure. Common clinical manifestations include rashes, joint pain (arthralgia), fever, swelling of lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy), shock, low blood pressure (hypotension), and an enlarged spleen (splenomegaly). Treatment for serum sickness is often supportive, as symptoms generally resolve on their own. In severe cases, corticosteroids may be prescribed to reduce inflammation. Antihistamines can also be used to alleviate symptoms.
